page: Amazon Web Services m5.4xlarge is a general-purpose Nitro hypervisor-based instance configured with a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio. It runs on an Intel Xeon 8175M x86_64 processor clocked at 3.1 GHz, delivering 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 8 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Memory provisioning includes 64.0 GB of DDR4 RAM operating at 3 GHz, allocating 4.0 GB of memory per vCPU. Hardware instruction extensions include AVX, AVX-512F, AES, and FMA, alongside an L3 cache capacity of 33 MB.

The hardware configuration includes no integrated local storage and no dedicated GPU accelerators, requiring reliance on external Amazon EBS volumes for persistent disk storage. Networking interfaces provide a baseline network bandwidth of 5 Gbps without bundled complimentary public IPv4 addresses. Memory subsystem testing reflects standard enterprise throughput, reaching 87.77 GB/s in large-block read operations and 45.25 GB/s in large-block write operations, with cached small-block reads peaking at 753.13 GB/s.

Benchmark evaluations indicate consistent middle-tier multi-threaded compute and throughput capabilities alongside subdued single-threaded performance. Single-core tests such as stress-ng (1282.29) and Geekbench (1034.0) fall into the lower quartile, as do single-threaded compression algorithms like gzip and bzip3. In contrast, multi-threaded tasks sit in the middle 50% percentile, with Geekbench multi-core reaching 6542.0 and PassMark CPU scoring 14441.4. Operational benchmarks show sustained application-tier performance, producing 13.15 million Redis SET operations per second and 11.92 GB/s static web serving throughput.

From a cost efficiency perspective, m5.4xlarge provides stable resource density for scalable microservices and database engines that benefit from balanced compute and memory distribution rather than isolated peak single-thread execution speeds. The instance is suited for enterprise application servers, mid-sized relational and in-memory databases, Clang-based software build environments, and containerized microservice clusters.
